title: Learn with your AI
bullets: Context, communication, checking, and building for your learning.
Week 6 · Learn, Vibe, Build · October 5, 2026
notes: Teach the substantive slides first, then one open live conversation with Claude, then small-group work. No timed demo interruptions.

title: What your recent builds taught us
bullets: The AI can finish a prompt and still miss the design you intended.
A page can look finished while its buttons do not work.
A local link or a repo alone is not a published website.
notes: Grounded in actual Week 4/5 submissions: visual intent failed to translate; one build had non-clickable cards; localhost and deployment-permission confusion persisted. Public slides deliberately omit names and private quotes.

title: Use AI to learn about AI
bullets: Ask for an explanation, an example, and a question to check your understanding.
Say what you already know: “I know HTML; Git is new to me.”
Compare its explanation with your source—not just how confident it sounds.
notes: Students recently asked their tools to explain the tool itself while building. Model this as a learning practice, not outsourcing understanding.

title: The reading: your AI as a coach
bullets: Arielle Shipper · “How to Get Better at AI by Asking AI” · Every
Ask where you are on the Eight Levels of AI Adoption, with evidence from your work.
Ask for one next step, then: “Teach me that and help me practise.”
notes: Assigned reading. Shipper turned reflection on actual projects into a coaching conversation. The reading link is in students’ accounts; no new due date.

title: No long chat history? Bring your own evidence
bullets: Paste your last two submissions or describe a recent project.
Ask: “What can I do already? Show examples. What should I learn next?”
Treat the AI’s assessment as a suggestion; correct its assumptions.
notes: Free plans need not have long-term memory. Give a small truthful sample, not every private conversation.

title: Markdown: readable, portable text
bullets: A .md file is a plain-text file—not a special app or database.
A little punctuation adds structure: headings, lists, links, code.
Read it in an editor, render it as a page, or paste it into your AI.
notes: Explain portability: the same text works across tools. A file can be edited without a platform account.

title: Markdown you can read and write
bullets: # Project notes
## What I want to learn
- Explain commits before changing files.
[Course lesson](https://cu.learnvibe.build/lessons/week-6/)
Use `git status` to see what changed.
notes: Point out # and ## headings; - list; [label](URL) link; backticks for code. These are examples, not a context template.
extra: Headings, lists, links, and code—with plain text underneath.

title: Context: what the AI can actually see
bullets: Its answer depends on the messages, files and tool results available now.
It does not automatically know your audience, preferences or project history.
“Improve my site” is weaker than a clear audience, goal and example.
notes: Avoid claiming every app literally starts at zero: some add saved memory or project files. Ask what context the tool loaded.

title: Save project context instead of repeating it
bullets: Write down what the project is, who it is for, and what should stay true.
Keep it short, correct and editable; update it when the project changes.
Example: “For nervous first-time visitors. Plain HTML/CSS. Do not invent event dates.”
notes: These are useful questions, not a rigid template or pair interview. Student projects vary: portfolios, creative work, tools, simulations.

title: Automatic loading is tool-specific
bullets: Codex uses AGENTS.md; Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md.
Other tools have their own rules and supported filenames—check yours.
In a chat app, paste the context or add it to a Project; it may not read local files.
notes: Do not imply any file name works universally. Our tested Claude Code installation also found AGENTS.md, but teach documented primary filenames. A fresh-session question can reveal whether the tool saw the file.

title: An index points to deeper context
bullets: A small index says which files exist and what each is for.
Example: docs/facts.md → verified facts; docs/design.md → visual direction.
The AI can open the relevant document instead of receiving one giant prompt.
notes: Index files are a map, not evidence that the AI read the linked files. Ask it which sources it used.

title: Describe the design, not just the features
bullets: “Make it better” leaves the visual choices to the model.
Name the audience, feeling, hierarchy and interactions you want.
Example: “Calm portfolio. Work first, muted colours, clickable project cards.”
notes: Week 4/5 reflections describe trouble communicating aesthetics; a recent rebuild improved when the student described the feeling instead of only listing features.

title: Make your feedback observable
bullets: Give a reference or screenshot; say what to keep and what to change.
Instead of “It’s broken”: “Clicking this card should open the project; nothing happens.”
Ask for one small change, then compare the result with your intention.
notes: Recent Week 5 work caught non-clickable cards through use. Specific observed behavior gives the agent something testable.

title: Debugging: find the mismatch
bullets: A bug is a difference between expected and observed behavior.
Reproduce it: what exact actions cause it? Capture the error or screenshot.
Ask the AI for a cause and a small fix; rerun the same check afterward.
notes: Do not blindly rewrite the whole app. Before a risky fix, save a working version. Recent students used AI for testing/debugging but still needed to notice what failed.

title: Check the experience—not just the code
bullets: Open it on a phone. Click every important button and link.
Try empty input, a strange answer, or a first-time visitor’s path.
For a learning tool, check its facts and quiz answers against a trustworthy source.
notes: A running build is not proof it is correct or useful. This transfers directly to the small-group learning builds.

title: When free credits run out
bullets: Save files and a short note: what works, what failed, what to try next.
Use that note to continue in a fresh session or another tool.
Reduce the request: one change or one explanation at a time.
notes: Recent Week 5 submissions described switching tools and running out of credits. Persistent context is a practical continuity aid; do not imply unlimited free usage.

title: Folder, repository, website: different things
bullets: Local folder: files on your own computer.
Git repository: those files plus a recorded history of versions.
Deployment: a published version that other people can open.
notes: A GitHub repo can hold code without having a live website. A folder path cannot be submitted as an accessible build link.

title: Commit, push, deploy: three actions
bullets: Commit saves a version and a message in your local Git history.
Push sends your commits to the repository on GitHub.
Deploy publishes the project through a host such as GitHub Pages or Vercel.
notes: Use an ordinary change as an example: fix a heading, commit “Clarify heading”, push, wait for deployment, verify the live page.

title: Your link must work on someone else’s phone
bullets: file:///… and localhost:8000 point to your own computer—not a public site.
A GitHub repository URL shows source; it may not be the live app URL.
Use the deployed HTTPS URL; test it on another device or in a private window.
notes: Repeated local-link issues in actual submissions. For a public build, check that it does not require your account to open.

title: A practical path to publishing
bullets: GitHub Desktop: create a repository → commit → publish to GitHub.
Plain HTML/CSS: GitHub Settings → Pages → main branch / root → Save.
A framework app may need Vercel: allow repository access, deploy, then test the URL.
notes: Recent Week 5 publishing confusion was partly Vercel needing GitHub repo access. Do not prescribe Pages for every framework app; the handout is supplemental detail, not essential to the invitation.

title: API, connector, MCP: what is the difference?
bullets: API: a service’s menu of requests that another program can make.
Connector: a bridge that lets your AI reach a service or files.
MCP: a shared protocol for AI apps to use tools; an MCP server may call an API.
notes: Example: weather service API returns a forecast; an AI connector calls it for a conversation. Conceptual only: no course server URL, setup or connector demo this week.

title: Access is a choice: read versus write
bullets: Read access can expose data; write access can change or delete it.
Give only the access needed; review changes before publishing or sending.
Keep keys, passwords and private data out of public files and repositories.
notes: Tools extend what the AI can do, not what it should be allowed to do. Responsibilities remain with the person using it. Four Ds stay implicit.

title: Bring this lesson into your own AI
bullets: Open cu.learnvibe.build → Everything for Week 6.
Click “Copy lesson as markdown”; paste it into Claude or another AI.
Ask: “Teach me this and quiz me”—then ask follow-ups in your own words.
notes: Every essential access instruction is here, not hidden in a handout. This is how the reading’s coaching idea becomes something students can do tonight.

title: After the slides: one conversation with Claude
bullets: Aaron will paste the lesson and talk through it with Claude.
The conversation may lead to building a little thing.
Watch how questions, context and checking shape the result.
notes: This is the only live demo slot, after the teaching content. Do not prescribe a project, script or output. If delayed, discuss a question from the lesson and move to group work.

title: In small groups: build for your learning
bullets: Choose a topic you want to understand or practise, and your own approach.
Make a quiz, interactive explainer, practice tool—or an idea of your own.
Use your AI; try the first version yourselves; check it and revise.
notes: Open-ended invitation, no fixed template or prescribed roles. Help students choose a small first learning goal without deciding their project for them.

title: How to start—and what to share
bullets: Give your AI the lesson, your learning question, or both.
Ask for a small first version. Test whether it actually helps you learn.
Show what you made, what you learned, and one thing you checked or changed.
notes: Optional: ask your AI what it needs to know about your project; save the useful context in markdown. Students can find the lesson from the preceding slide. No due date added.
